report:
### Conclusion
The health claim that food-grade wax coatings on apples cause cancer is unsupported by scientific evidence. Regulatory agencies and food safety experts agree that food-grade waxes applied to produce are non-toxic, digestible, and safe to eat.

### Evidence Overview
* **Regulatory Approval:** The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approves natural and food-grade waxes—such as carnauba wax, shellac, and beeswax—for direct application to produce. These coatings have been safely used for decades to replace natural fruit wax, seal in moisture, and prevent spoilage (http://nwhort.org/fruitcoatings/).
* **Expert Safety Consensus:** Food safety experts widely confirm that commercial, food-grade waxes applied to apples pose no toxicity or health risks to humans (https://wellnd.com/is-apple-wax-safe-to-eat). 
* **Origin of Cancer Claims:** Alarmist claims often stem from viral social media misinformation or specific additive concerns, such as morpholine (an emulsifier used in some wax formulations to aid application). Although morpholine can theoretically convert to nitrosomorpholine under specific conditions, realistic human exposure from the minute quantities on fruit wax does not present a practical cancer risk (https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/critical-thinking-health-and-nutrition/waxing-lyrical-about-fruit-wax).
* **Minimal Intake:** Commercial wax is applied extremely sparingly—typically just a drop or two per apple—making dietary exposure negligible (https://www.mashed.com/1761304/should-you-be-worried-about-wax-on-apples/).

Consumers wishing to reduce their intake of waxes or surface dirt can simply wash or peel their produce, though eating the food-grade wax is harmless.
